articles.title_orig: China-hawk Philippine defence chief open to presidential bid
articles.title_zh: China-hawk Philippine defence chief open to presidential bid
articles.content_orig:
By Andreo Calonzo and Philip J Heijmans
(Bloomberg) — Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said he's open to a presidential run in 2028, potentially pitting the China hawk against current Vice President Sara Duterte.
"If I have a chance, maybe. If I don't, forget it," Teodoro said in an interview with Bloomberg News on Friday (30 Oct). President Ferdinand Marcos Jr can't run for reelection then because of term limits.
Teodoro has been among the most vocal critics of China's military buildup in the South China Sea. Beijing slapped sanctions on him earlier this year, barring him from entering the mainland, Hong Kong and Macau.
The defence chief has also been at the forefront of the Philippines' efforts to strengthen its defense alliance with the US. Under his watch, the Southeast Asian nation has hosted American weaponry, and implemented the expansion of US forces' access to military sites near two regional flashpoints: Taiwan and the South China Sea.
Early polls, however, show that victory for Teodoro will be a long shot. Sara, daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, is by far the leading candidate for the next presidential election, even as she faces an impeachment trial in the Senate, which could bar her from politics for life if convicted.
Teodoro, 62, ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 2010.
During the interview, the defence chief also said the Southeast Asian nation's next leadership should be cautious about Chinese money, recalling how Rodrigo Duterte's administration built closer ties with Beijing.
"There was accommodation already, not merely cooperation," Teodoro said. "What happened? We were suddenly populated internally by illegal Chinese activities in the guise of investments."
To be sure, he added that not all Chinese investments were bad, particularly "those that have undergone appropriate due diligence processes." But he did caution investments on critical infrastructure "because we have a national dispute with an aggressive neighbour."
Teodoro met with US counterpart Pete Hegseth this week in Cebu, where they agreed to fast-track the Philippine military's modernisation. The meeting was held on the sidelines of a summit among Southeast Asia's defense leaders, where the US pushed for a defence cooperation framework as it counters China's presence in the region.
For Teodoro, the US remains to be a reliable partner for the Philippines, even as alliances across the world are tested under President Donald Trump. Washington values the Philippines' unique geography straddling the South China Sea and the Pacific Ocean, according to the defense chief.
"The commitment of Hegseth is a visible sign of support. President Trump has reiterated it several times," Teodoro said. "Not only in words, but in deed."

articles.title_orig: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto hack
articles.title_zh: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto hack
articles.content_orig:
Binance customers withdrew a net $3.64bn (£2.72bn) of assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following a record hack last week .
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber attack , which is said to be the largest hack in history.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach, but that the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
"Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion," Binance posted on X.
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
It also said withdrawals for more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .
The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it has not been affected by the issue.
The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.
Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The crypto withdrawn represents just a fraction of the total value of assets held by Binance.
The exact valuation of Binance is unclear as the firm is privately held, though the company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets in its custody.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.34bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.
Binance said it replaced customers' assets using a combination of channels that include its corporate treasury and its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash: four US citizens, and nationals from Japan, Canada among dead, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash: four US citizens, and nationals from Japan, Canada among dead, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards
Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.
The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.
The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

articles.title_orig: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
articles.title_zh: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
articles.content_orig:
Binance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3 billion hack, as customers rushed to move funds off the platform.
The exchange processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC on Nov. 1, Binance said in a post on X.
The resulting net outflows represented 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets, based on its latest available proof-of-reserves data as of Oct. 28.
Binance said withdrawal volumes had declined and were stabilizing following an initial spike, while deposit volumes remained substantial.
The exchange began restoring withdrawals in phases at 6 a.m. UTC on Sunday, with services resuming across all 15 networks and assets included in the initial phase by 12:36 p.m. UTC. It said testing was continuing for the remaining networks and assets.
Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao sought to reassure users following the breach, writing on X that "98% choose to stay!" He said most of the net outflows occurred within the first couple of hours after withdrawals resumed. "Trust isn't earned by what you say in good times. It's earned by what you do in hard times," Zhao added.
The withdrawals followed a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance last week. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor.
The exchange has said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass the losses on to users.
Binance said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The exchange said the remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that would take longer to source in the quantities required.

A month ago, a series of news reports said oil flows out of Hormuz had recovered to pre-war levels, pushing oil prices lower. However, the rout did not last. Benchmarks are set for their fourth monthly gain in a row, and no amount of repeating that Gulf states are exporting even more oil than before the war can change that. Because barrels are not the whole story.
“What is the price of oil? Eight months into the war with Iran , what should be a straightforward question has become surprisingly hard to answer,” JP Morgan’s head of global commodities, Natasha Kaneva, said as quoted by the Wall Street Journal this week. The publication noted that Kaneva’s own oil price model suggests a fair value of $94 for a barrel of Brent crude.
Yet Brent crude is trading at over $116 per barrel.
This is only confusing on the surface. Below it, we find an abundance of risks for those shipping crude oil out of the Persian Gulf, dozens of tankers getting hit with drones or missiles in the past few weeks, and a shortage of tankers resulting from Saudi Arabia’s shift to ship-to-ship transfers off the coast of Oman to reduce the risk of having its tankers blown up in Hormuz or the Red Sea.
Stemming from all this is the issue of shipping costs for crude oil produced in the Middle East. These have soared to all-time highs and prompted producing countries to discount their oil in order to stimulate demand—even though all those reports about improving oil flows in the Persian Gulf served to pressure oil prices. This is because those flows cannot be sustained, not in an environment where the risk of a missile attack is so high. Related: Japan to Overtake China As World’s Top LNG Importer This Year
“This recovery has coincided with a sharp deterioration in maritime security as vessels remain exposed to attacks and insurance and freight costs have risen sharply,” UBS commodity strategist Giovanni Staunovo said, as quoted by the Wall Street Journal.
The war premium on oil, in other words, is alive and well. Yet it is not the only factor driving prices. In the early weeks of the war, some observers were surprised that oil prices were not soaring higher. Indeed, the initial reaction of the oil market to the war was a really optimistic one. Traders—and pretty much everyone else—were sure it wouldn’t last more than a few weeks, and the world was awash with oil, so it had a solid supply cushion.
Yet that modest price increase only took place on the futures market. On the physical market, oil surged. It took several months for futures and physical prices to begin converging, but it appears this is what might be happening right now, with physical prices off their highs from earlier this year. The problem for those hoping for sub-$100 Brent is that eight months into the war, the global supply cushion is gone, the prospect for peace remains elusive, and drivers are paying record-high prices for diesel. The price of oil is reflecting all of this, unlike it did three months ago, when it was being moved primarily by President Trump’s Truth Social posts and reports citing unnamed sources as saying peace was close.
Oil prices currently reflect the reality that the world’s energy supply crunch is not going to be over soon. Even the head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, said earlier this week the disruption will likely continue well into next year. “I am afraid I don't see any credible pathway that the markets will go next year, where we were before this war has started,” Birol said. He also said the crisis would fuel the acceleration of what he called “The Age of Electricity,” but some have doubts about it—electricity prices are still quite closely tied to the prices of the hydrocarbons that generate most of the world’s electricity.
In addition to all existing trends and developments, prices are stuck above $100 per barrel because of the anticipation of future developments, and more specifically the potential escalation between the United States, Israel, and Iran. President Trump has on several occasions admitted he was considering a return to hostilities after the November 3 rd midterms. Iran has responded with its own threats that any return to a hot war would prompt retaliation. In other words, both sides are ready to resume fighting, despite ongoing efforts at diplomacy from Gulf states and Pakistan.
The midterms are next Tuesday. What follows after them is anyone’s guess but it appears most expect a renewal of hostilities in the Persian Gulf. And that means a higher war premium and a further extension of the energy supply disruption that has become the defining event of this year. Whatever analyst models may suggest, prices are going to stay higher until there is a clear sign that peace is a real possibility.
By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo cracks are real, and Apple's 'small number' may not be so small
articles.content_orig:
In a memo shared with Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers this week, and later obtained by MacRumors , Apple provided technicians with guidance on how to diagnose and address the iPhone Duo's inner display cracking issue.
If a customer reports the issue, Apple advised technicians to inspect the iPhone Duo and repair or replace it in accordance with their standard procedures. While the instructions themselves are straightforward, the fact that Apple issued an internal memo suggests the issue is widespread enough to warrant official guidance.
Apple's memo said the issue affects a small number of iPhone Duo units, which is consistent with what it said in a public statement on Monday.
"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," said Apple, in a statement shared with MacRumors . If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement." You can get support on Apple's website or by calling 1-800-APL-CARE in the U.S. and Canada.
Apple said most iPhone Duo units are not susceptible to this issue and that impacted units appear to exhibit the defects rather quickly after usage.
Apple said there is no iPhone Duo recall, and the company has yet to launch a public-facing repair program on its website for this issue.
Almost immediately after the iPhone Duo began arriving to customers a week ago, a handful of early adopters reported that the device's inner display had cracked , resulting in lines appearing down the middle and towards the right side of the screen.
The electronics repair website iFixit completed an iPhone Duo teardown and said that the issue is likely related to a defective hinge on affected units. However, Apple has yet to comment on the underlying cause of the issue.

Russia and Ukraine completed a remarkably successful humanitarian mission in occupied Kherson Oblast, as some Ukrainian civilians returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory. Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets noted that the Oleshky ceasefire is the longest localized ceasefire that both sides have observed since 2022.[1] Lubinets and Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova reported on October 30 and 31 that some residents of occupied Kherson Oblast, particularly from Oleshky, returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory, while others chose to stay in the area or travelled to occupied Simferopol, Crimea.[2] Ukrainian officials reported on October 31 that residents of Oleshky and nearby settlements flew to Belarus and then crossed the border into Chernihiv Oblast.[3] This humanitarian mission was remarkable in that Lubinets traveled to occupied Oleshky and Russia then back to Ukraine, Oleshky residents received humanitarian aid, and at least some civilians successfully evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled areas. The exact number of Oleshky residents who were able to leave the settlement and return to Ukrainian-controlled territory remains unclear as of this writing. ISW will provide further details on this humanitarian operation in the forthcoming Russian Occupation Update.
Both Russian and Ukrainian forces appear to have largely abided by the terms of the localized ceasefire in occupied Kherson Oblast since it came into effect on the morning of October 27, although there are limited allegations of ceasefire violations. Ukrainian Southern Group of Forces Spokesperson Maksym Kravchuk reported on October 31 that Russian forces repeatedly violated the terms of the ceasefire, including by using reconnaissance drones and dropping explosives from drones on Ukrainian positions.[4] Russian Ambassador-at-Large and former Russian occupation official Rodion Miroshnik claimed on October 31 that Ukrainian forces struck a civilian vehicle with a drone on the outskirts of Oleshky on October 31.[5] ISW is unable to independently verify these claimed ceasefire violations, but it appears that the humanitarian mission was nonetheless largely successful.
Kravchuk also noted on October 31 that Russian forces are taking advantage of the localized ceasefire in Oleshky to conduct personnel rotations, strengthen their positions and logistics, evacuate wounded and killed servicemembers, and install protection against Ukrainian drones on roads in the area.[6]
The Kremlin is refusing to compromise on its original maximalist demands from 2022 while continuing to ignore Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s offers of large-scale frontline ceasefires as Russia’s losses grow disproportionately to its territorial gains. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on October 30 told reporters at the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting that Russia’s position on a peace settlement in Ukraine is well-known and has remained unchanged since the start of the full-scale invasion.[7] Lavrov reiterated Russia’s claimed “root causes” of the war, including the alleged discrimination against ethnic Russians and the Russian language and the spread of neo-Nazism in Ukraine. Kremlin officials have repeatedly reaffirmed their maximalist objectives throughout the war while refusing Ukrainian- and US-proposed temporary ceasefires and compromises. Ukraine and the United States first proposed an immediate 30-day ceasefire along the entire frontline on March 11, 2025.[8] The Kremlin rejected that and subsequent proposed ceasefires, and Russian forces have suffered at least 698,000 casualties and gained just over 4,000 square kilometers (about the total area of Rhode Island) since then.[9]
The Kremlin is attempting to portray Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russia as the obstacle to peace talks — the latest Russian effort to falsely blame Ukraine for Russia’s refusal to meaningfully engage in negotiations. Lavrov complained on October 30 about Ukraine’s long-range strikes deep into the Russian rear and claimed that these strikes do not signal that Ukraine is preparing for negotiations.[10] Lavrov’s statement ignores Russia’s own daily long-range strike campaigns against Ukraine and the Kremlin’s repeated rejections of US- and Ukrainian-proposed moratoriums on long-range strikes against energy infrastructure.[11] The Kremlin has used Ukrainian strikes — real and alleged — to deflect blame away from Russia for stalled peace negotiations, including after the claimed strike against Russian President Vladimir Putin’s residence in Novgorod Oblast in December 2025 and the strike against occupied Khorly, Kherson Oblast in January 2026.[12]
The Kremlin continues to try to push European leaders out of peace talks, despite Russian demands that a peace settlement restructure the European security architecture. The US Department of State approved the possible sale of 500 PAC-3 Patriot ballistic missile interceptors to Ukraine, but the delivery will reportedly not occur for several years. [16] Various Western outlets, citing unidentified sources, reported that the approval is for the delivery of newly manufactured interceptors, which is not expected until after 2030.[17] The sale therefore will not support Ukraine’s efforts to defend itself during the expected intense Russian ballistic missile strike campaign in Winter 2026-2027. Ukraine’s vulnerability resulting from insufficient ballistic missile interceptor supplies will encourage Russian President Vladimir Putin to pursue his current theory of victory that aims to use ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to force a Ukrainian surrender through a decisive long-range strike campaign over this coming winter.[18]

articles.title_orig: Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote
articles.title_zh: Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote
articles.content_orig:
The head of Israel’s elections commission has said the results of the country’s general election would still stand even if claims of foreign interference were substantiated.
“Our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole,” Central Elections Committee head Noam Sohlberg said in a video on Sunday, in which he appeared with the head of the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, and the attorney general.
Prime Minister Benyamin Netanyahu’s Likud party had questioned the results after saying, without providing evidence, that Arab-led parties, which made significant gains in Tuesday’s elections, “stole” the vote and accepted funding from Qatar to do it.
Qatar has rejected the allegations , calling it a disinformation campaign.
Also on Sunday, Israeli police released two out of three political activists arrested before Tuesday’s polls opened. They were carrying envelopes of cash, allegedly to bribe voters, police said.
One was released on unspecified conditions, while another was ordered to remain on house arrest.
Police said the suspects were connected to the Arab-led Ra’am party, which won eight seats.
Its leader, Mansour Abbas, denounced the arrests as undemocratic and “an attempt to influence the election results”.
Main opposition leader Eisenkot on Sunday accused Netanyahu of launching an “orchestrated and organised campaign to delegitimise the results”.
Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Arab parties, but a deadlock in Tuesday’s elections means siding with the parties could help him form a government.
Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s elections, while the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, won 48, meaning neither side can form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament alone.
Israel’s three Arab-led parties, including the Ra’am party, won a record 19 seats.
A coalition of Arab parties with Eisenkot would provide a comfortable majority of 67 in parliament. However, for many in Israel, the idea of siding with Arab parties is politically unpalatable.
The results are due to be officially certified this week, after which President Isaac Herzog must nominate a candidate to form a new government.

articles.title_orig: Queen's Domain Review
articles.title_zh: Queen's Domain Review
articles.content_orig:
Usually games don't wear their inspirations on their sleeve as clearly as Queen's Domain . The name says it all; Freshly Baked Games really, really like King's Field and wanted to make their own take on the idea - as has become a bit of a small trend in recent years.
You're a Prince, and after trying to follow your Father the King in his quest to defeat the evil resurrected Queen who is also the mortal avatar of a God of the Void you shipwreck and are forced to pick up the pieces of an expedition gone horribly wrong and to succeed where the King and his Knights have failed.
Combat is simple; you have a stamina meter, and you can run indefinitely; however, your primary and secondary attacks scale off your current stamina, so you can't just run around forever taking potshots on enemies. You have to choose wisely when to stop and let it replenish before dipping in to strike an enemy. Different enemies have weaknesses to various attack types - slash, strike, and pierce - so it's best to use the right weapon for the job.
You can have up to 3 secondary weapons - daggers, chakrams or other throwables - and 3 primary weapons equipped. Secondaries don't use stamina, but will recharge over time. Regardless of what you have equipped, very shortly into the adventure you'll gain access to a sword blessed with "Wind Gems", which is the main driving factor for much of Queen's Domain's level design.
While combat is very deliberate as one might expect from the genre, platforming is the name of the game here and is facilitated by the ability to airdash to cross gaps, reach distant ledges, or search for secrets halfway down pits and the like. At first, players will only have access to one Wind Gem, and one airdash, at a time; but as you progress through the game you'll gain access to more gems, giving you multiple airdashes and as such more options for places to explore.
It's an inspired mechanic, and once it sets in just how much of the world is truly accessible to you, Queen's Domain's world ends up feeling unlike any other RPG I've played. Secrets are tucked everywhere; hidden walls with your only clues being skeletons of others using their last moments to offer a hint to their existence, or others where lenses you can discover of the game's many gods offer assistance in seeking them out. See a ledge? Chances are if you can reach it, there's something there worth your while.
A great example of this are weapons; use them enough and they'll level up, increasing their stats. Rusty weapons will evolve into a unique weapon after you've trudged along with them enough; others might undergo a different transformation entirely. One Trident I received early on had an interesting description, and after enough use my suspicions were confirmed. Even if the battle system itself is simple, there's an insane level of player expression available across the dozens of weapons to find across the world or purchase at the game's trader outpost.
If all you want to do is reach the game's first ending you'll be looking at a 20 or so hour adventure; straightforward enough, but still requiring players to be inquisitive with how they proceed. Yet if you want to seek out the game's additional endings, it slowly dawns on you just how vast of a scope the game is hiding, and how many areas you may have thought you've thoroughly explored still have left to discover.
This is usually a good thing, though I do think nearing the ending of the game it gets a bit much; something it feels that Freshly Baked Games themselves agreed with, considering some concessions they make as you approach the home stretch. I can't say I'm the biggest fan of how some collectibles necessary for the True Ending I'd almost definitely never would have found otherwise. With how well the game was at giving you hints up until this point, it especially stings.
That being said, I'd wager that most players won't have quite as challenging a time finding the secrets as I did; now that the game is out, it feels obvious that Queen's Domain is meant as much of a communal affair as a solo delve. Even when I started to grow tired of combing over areas again, the game's visual identity remained striking enough that I never truly got bored of it all. While Queen's Domain doesn't actually look like an original PlayStation game - with the visual fidelity and view distance on display, I doubt it would run smoothly on a PlayStation 3 or 4, even - it evokes the feeling while maintaining an identity of its own.
Queen's Domain is something special, and of all the King's Field inspired RPGs in recent memory it clearly establishes itself as the best in its class. If you're willing to play to its rules, Queen's Domain isn't just one of the best RPGs of the year, but a genuine must play.

By Jonathan Swan Maggie Haberman Ana Swanson Paul Mozur Tripp Mickle and Julian E. Barnes
American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence.
A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing.
But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive.
For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump’s, set off alarms at the White House.
Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.
This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts.
American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A.I. chips.

Good evening. If all had gone according to plan, the United States v Wanzhou Meng and Huawei Technologies would have opened in a federal courtroom in the waning months of President Donald Trump’s first term. And what a trial it would have been: an heir to one of China’s most successful and strategically important companies, detained in Canada and extradited to the U.S., on trial for allegedly lying to banks about Huawei operations in Iran that were in violation of American sanctions on the country. But Xi Jinping forestalled that humiliating spectacle by ordering the arrest of two Canadians in China, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, and not releasing them until the U.S. and Canada allowed Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, to return to China in September 2021. Five years later the United States v Huawei Technologies , minus Meng, is finally underway. Noah Berman reports from the courtroom in Brooklyn.
In other articles, Leon Panetta speaks with Bob Davis about his dealings with China as a Congressman, White House Chief-of-Staff, CIA Director and Secretary of Defense.
Noah Berman on DayOne , the Singaporean data center operator that is helping Chinese companies realise their AI ambitions.
In The Big Picture , Savannah Billman writes about the enormous popularity of AI-generated “short dramas” in China.
Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin on the barriers to a common-sense Sino-U.S. AI safety agreement .
And finally, be sure to catch up on the latest episode of our weekly podcast , with Peiyue Wu talking about her recent cover on dual-use farms in China.
Want this emailed directly to your inbox? Sign up to receive our free newsletter.
In 2021 Meng Wanzhou, daughter of Huawei Technologies founder Ren Zhengfei, signed a “statement of facts” to resolve U.S. charges against her. According to that statement, “Ms. Meng [told HSBC] … Huawei’s relationship with Skycom was ‘normal business cooperation’ and … she described Skycom as a … ‘third party Huawei works with’ in Iran … Those statements were untrue because, as Ms. Meng knew, … Huawei controlled Skycom.” The U.S. let Meng go regardless because the Chinese government made it clear that it would not release two Canadian hostages until she was freed. Five years later the U.S. government’s case against Huawei is finally underway in New York, with Meng safely back in China.
Leon Panetta fought with, and engaged with China over a long career in politics. The former Congressman, White House Chief of Staff, CIA Director and Defense Secretary talks with Bob Davis about why China thinks President Trump is good for China.
“If China senses weakness, they’ll take advantage of it,” Panetta says. “Right now, China is in a stronger position because we’re locked in a war in Iran, our economy is being impacted by that war, and there’s a lot of unpredictability about the U.S. China has been able to take advantage in areas where once we had some influence, particularly in the Pacific.”
Illustration by Lauren Crow
The U.S. government doesn’t want America’s best chips to power Chinese data centers that would then help Chinese companies hone their AI models and applications. DayOne, a Singapore-based data center provider, profits from this by building data centers in Southeast Asia where Chinese AI firms can legally access America’s best chips. Noah Berman looks at DayOne and the IPO prospectus it has just issued. “DayOne’s rise,” he writes, “illustrates how companies can profit, and even gain backing from American investors, as U.S. export controls lead Chinese companies to seek access to data centers overseas.”
Are you, like the Old Dad who writes this newsletter, also a parent who dreads the short videos on YouTube and elsewhere that so easily reel in your kids? Alas, writes Savannah Billman , if China is anything to go by — as it increasingly is when it comes to tech trends — the madness is only going to get worse. Almost 900 million (!) Chinese people are watching AI-generated “short dramas”, issued as a seemingly endless stream of two-minute videos, on a new generation of apps tailored to the new genre. Over the first half of this year alone about 267,000 AI short videos were released. Ugh.
Recent steps taken towards the establishment of a U.S.-China AI incident-reporting channel are important, write Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin . But, they add, there is “a more pressing issue: frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they need”.

articles.title_orig: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
articles.title_zh: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
articles.content_orig:
A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.
The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.
On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack.
The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.
In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.
Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.
Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".
He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.
The limited pause in hostilities, which started on Tuesday, was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo.
It was originally confined to the city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and was expanded across the wider region of Kherson.
Oleshky had been trapped on one side by the Dnipro river and the other by Russian forces, with routes out mined and subject to drone attack.
Residents trapped there were suffering severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
The truce allowed for Oleskhy residents to evacuate if they wanted, and there were emotional scenes on Saturday of reunions between loved ones who hadn't seen eachother for years.
There are Ukrainian military positions just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border.
The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.

Acting President Iliana Iotova is the apparent winner of Bulgaria’s presidential run-off, according to initial results, as her rival has conceded defeat.
Iotova, who advocates for dialogue with Russia and opposes military aid to Ukraine, received 58 percent of the vote in Sunday’s run-off , according to several polling agencies’ counts.
If confirmed by official results, she would become Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state.
Her opponent, former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, is said to be trailing at about 38 percent.
Gyurov, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, said the results had to be accepted as they stood.
“This is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted,” he said.
Exit polls put voter participation at about 27 to 29 percent, slightly higher ‌than the first-round race last week, which had a record-low turnout of 23 percent.
Official results are expected on Monday as ballots are counted for the presidency, which is largely ceremonial.
Iotova, 61, took over as acting president in January, when her longtime ally, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, resigned to run in, and win, a parliamentary election.
“I don’t like either of the two candidates,” Krassimira Kostova, a 64-year-old teacher in the capital, Sofia, who voted anyway, told the AFP news agency.
Petar Doitchinov, a 67-year-old retired engineer, said he had skipped the first round last week because he expected a run-off. He said he voted for “the lesser evil”, as neither candidate matched his “vision of democracy”.
The vote comes as 21 people remain missing following a series of drone attacks last month on commercial vessels off the country’s Black Sea coast. They are suspected to be spillover from Russia’s war on Ukraine.
Prime Minister Radev has said the attacks appear to serve Moscow’s interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, though his government said there was no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.
Both presidential candidates have condemned the attacks and called for a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.
Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister, criticised Iotova in a television debate for not explicitly blaming Russia. “Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken,” he said.
Iotova said that “peace can come only through negotiations”. After voting, she said she wanted “Bulgaria to be strong in a strong Europe” and “sovereign in its decisions”.
In the first round of voting last week , Iotova won 35 percent, with Gyurov on 32 percent, a much narrower gap than the 20-point lead opinion polls had predicted for Iotova.
Political analyst Teodor Slavev told the AFP news agency that voters were passing judgement on “Iotova’s unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea”.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says public air raid alert app sent false alerts after being hacked
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says public air raid alert app sent false alerts after being hacked
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainians are used to reacting to the warnings of Russian attacks sent via the air alert app
Ukraine's air raid alert app was apparently hacked on Sunday and for a short time said the capital Kyiv was subject to a radiation threat, the Ukrainian Air Force has said.
The alert on Telegram read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
The Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said there had been a failure in the app, and urged people to use other sources of information to clarify the situation on the threat of air strikes.
A few hours later Russian authorities said its app was hacked. A Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Russia has the world's biggest nuclear arsenal, and President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly suggested an openness to using all weapons at Russia's disposal .
The alerts, in Ukrainian, started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT), with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide. Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat.  Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48, which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying".
A third alert, at 22:49, again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49, a fourth alert stated there was a "Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
In a separate post on Telegram, the Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said that due to the Air Alert application, the Radiation Hazard signal was played on loudspeaker devices in the Lviv region, and added there was no threat of radiation hazard.
If the alert app is not working, Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation advises the public to turn on notifications on their smartphones, pay attention to sirens, and to only read official sources
Several leaders of other regions also posted on Telegram that the app had apparently been hacked and there was no local threat.
"Everything is calm in the region for now," said Svitlana Onyshchuk, the governor of the Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. The app had reported a red-level air raid alert for the oblast in Ukraine's east, between 22:50 and 23:57.
The Vinnytsia regional head, Natalya Zabolotna, said there had been a cyber-attack on the Air Alert app and posted a warning on Telegram not to click on the link in the message, which could be a phishing attempt.
The Air Alert app is supported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, and informs users instantly about the beginning and end of defence alerts. The ministry had earlier said the app was temporarily disabled for maintenance after it had "apparently been compromised". It urged residents to turn on their smartphones' emergency notifications so they could receive state-issued distress signals.
A few hours after the false alerts in Ukraine, Russia's ministry of emergency situations said its app had been subjected to "a massive cyberattack" which sent "fake information to the public".
No further details were given by the ministry or state media.
Ukrainian news outlet, UNN, reported the hack sent fake alerts of a nuclear threat inside Russia.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian held territory, said on its Telegram page that the app had been hacked, accompanied with laughing emojis.
A screenshot of a purported emergency alert published by Atesh, which has not been verified by the BBC, told users to "urgently" stock up on provisions for three weeks and take cover in basements. It also used obscene language. Atesh has been contacted for comment.
The alerts occurred just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region , which was implemented last Tuesday and officially ended at 23:00 Sunday.
Fighting had continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place, to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky .
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.title_zh: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.content_orig:
Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.
Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.
Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.
Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.
Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.
She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term.
"I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.
In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.
However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.
Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.
By the end of Thursday,  the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours  trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Wall Street's reaction to Microsoft's update was more muted, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers , which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

articles.title_orig: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.title_zh: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".
He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".
Browne went on to say his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.
She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."
The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK government's position".
The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation" , and that Britain "must face up to the past".
His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by King Charles, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.
Each biennial meeting has a theme and this year's is officially called Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.
Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba,  Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity".
"True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son the Duke of Sussex made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked if the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

articles.title_orig: Humans in The Andes Seem to Have Evolved an Unusual Genetic Ability
articles.title_zh: Humans in The Andes Seem to Have Evolved an Unusual Genetic Ability
articles.content_orig:
Over thousands of years, humans living high in the Argentinian Andes have relied on drinking water that would make most people deathly ill.
There, naturally occurring arsenic in volcanic bedrock leaches into the groundwater, contaminating the local water supply with levels of the toxic metalloid that would pose serious health risks to most human populations.
But for one group in northern Argentina, natural selection may have provided an unusual genetic advantage, research shows.
According to a DNA analysis of people across western South America, a population in the Argentinian Andes carries a gene variant that likely helps them metabolize arsenic more safely.
"Adaptation drives genomic changes; however, evidence of specific adaptations in humans remains limited," researchers wrote in a 2015 study led by evolutionary biologists Carina Schlebusch and Lucie Gattepaille of Uppsala University.
"Our data show that adaptation to tolerate the environmental stressor arsenic has likely driven an increase in the frequencies of protective variants of AS3MT, providing the first evidence of human adaptation to a toxic chemical."
Given enough time and gentle enough exposure to a hazard, life has shown a remarkable ability to adapt to all sorts of wild conditions – from extreme heat to complete lack of oxygen to dangerous radiation levels .
However, relatively little is known about how human populations adapt to toxic chemicals in their environment. Arsenic is highly toxic , associated with cancer, skin lesions, pregnancy complications, and early death.
It's also widespread, naturally present at high levels in the groundwater of many regions around the world.
The current recommended limit for arsenic in drinking water, set by the World Health Organization, is 10 micrograms per liter .
Until a filtration system was installed in 2012, the remote, high-altitude town of San Antonio de los Cobres , in Argentina's Puna de Atacama plateau, had drinking water that contained around 200 micrograms of arsenic per liter – about 20 times the recommended limit.
Yet the region has been inhabited for thousands of years – at least 7,000 years , and perhaps as long as 11,000.
This apparent ability to shrug off dangerously high arsenic levels puzzled scientists for decades.
In 1995, scientists noted that women from the Argentinian Andes had a "unique" ability to metabolize arsenic, as evidenced by metabolites in their urine.
When arsenic enters the body, enzymes convert it through several chemical forms .
One of these intermediate forms, called monomethylated arsenic (MMA), is particularly toxic. A later form, dimethylated arsenic (DMA), is easier for the body to excrete in urine.
People in San Antonio de los Cobres tended to produce less of the toxic intermediate and more of the easily excreted form, suggesting their bodies were unusually efficient at processing arsenic.
Intrigued, Schlebusch, Gattepaille, and their colleagues wanted to solve the puzzle at the genetic level.
The team analyzed DNA from blood samples or cheek swabs, taken from 124 women in San Antonio de los Cobres whose urine showed a wide range of arsenic metabolite levels.
They then examined millions of genetic markers across the genome.
To determine whether the gene variant was unique to the Argentine population, the researchers compared their results with publicly available genome data from Peru and Colombia, drawn from the international 1000 Genomes Project .
Previous research showed that an enzyme called arsenic (+3 oxidation state) methyltransferase (AS3MT) could play a key role in arsenic metabolism, so that is where the researchers focused their efforts.
What they found was a cluster of genetic variants near the AS3MT gene that strongly influenced how the body processes arsenic.
These variants were far more common in people from San Antonio de los Cobres than in genetically similar populations in Peru and Colombia.
It's not just the Andes, either.
A September 2025 study out of the University of Chicago, looking at more than 6,500 arsenic-exposed adults in Bangladesh, identified two more gene clusters – FMO and GSTO – that also shape how efficiently someone metabolizes arsenic, on top of the AS3MT variant.
The variants appear to make the body more efficient at converting arsenic into forms that can be safely excreted in urine, reducing the buildup of the most toxic intermediate compounds – a result that neatly aligns with earlier studies of arsenic metabolites in urine.
Related: Scientists Have Discovered Where Native Hawaiians Came From, And The Genetic Effect of Their Long Voyage
While arsenic contamination is common around the world, very few communities have lived with such high levels of exposure for long periods of time.
In San Antonio de los Cobres, people have lived with arsenic in their groundwater for thousands of years – long enough for natural selection to favor traits that reduce vulnerability to arsenic's toxic effects.
Later research suggests similar genetic signals may also appear in other Andean populations exposed to arsenic for generations, supporting the findings that long-term exposure can drive genetic tolerance, and hinting that the adaptation may be more widespread across the region.
"Given the severe deleterious health effects of arsenic in both children and adults," the researchers wrote , "individuals who carry the arsenic-tolerance haplotype… could have a very strong selective advantage in high-arsenic environments."
The research was published in Molecular Biology and Evolution .

articles.title_orig: Iran’s top diplomat hopes US shows ‘rationality,’ and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Iran’s top diplomat hopes US shows ‘rationality,’ and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
“Some progress” has been made in efforts to reach an agreement between the US and Iran, several sources familiar with the negotiations told The Jerusalem Post . However, the sources stressed that "significant gaps remain between the two sides".
“There is some optimism that an agreement can be reached. But there is still work to be done,” one source said.
Another source said no progress had been made on the nuclear issue and that the advances concerned other matters, including the timeline for implementing a potential agreement.
In recent days, Qatari mediators have intensified indirect diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran amid growing fears of a potential military escalation following the US midterm elections.
An Iranian delegation traveled to Doha for several days of talks, coordinated closely with Washington, following intensive consultations in Tehran. The discussions reportedly focus on proposals to de-escalate the eight-month-old conflict, including a potential two-day framework for reopening the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz and resuming broader peace negotiations.
Despite these diplomatic efforts, significant gaps remain between the two sides. Tehran is demanding that Washington lift recent sanctions, reinstate oil waivers, reduce its regional military presence, and end port blockades before addressing restrictions on Iran's nuclear program.
By contrast, US officials, following recent outreach by Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei , insist that any comprehensive agreement must address nuclear concerns from the outset.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump was asked how negotiations with Iran were progressing.
“They're going fine, but they're not very reliable. They make a deal and then they back out,” he responded.
Trump also said there were “one or two sites” in Iran's nuclear program that the US needed to address.
“But we can do that in 10 minutes,” he added.
A source familiar with the matter confirmed to the Post that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump spoke by phone on Saturday. The call came days after Trump was briefed by US Central Command (CENTCOM) commander Adm. Brad Cooper on military options for a possible operation against Iran.
Meanwhile, Iranian Deputy Parliament Speaker Ali Nikzad said Iran had no intention of negotiating over its nuclear program, regardless of the pressure exerted on it.
Dr. Raz Zimmt, head of the Iran and Shi'ite Axis Research Program at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Jerusalem Post that each side currently needs something from the other that cannot be reversed, while neither is willing to make what would constitute an irreversible concession.
“The Americans are prepared to lift the naval blockade and some of the sanctions, since these measures can be reinstated, and in return they are demanding something on the nuclear front, such as an inspectors' visit and/or action regarding the enriched uranium. The Iranians, meanwhile, are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and perhaps even allow inspectors to visit certain sites, but they are unwilling to give up their enriched uranium. Instead, they are demanding something permanent, such as the unfreezing of Iranian assets.
“I find it difficult to see how this deadlock can be resolved,” Zimmt said.
Nevertheless, he added that, given the risks of another round of military confrontation, he would not rule out the possibility that the two sides could ultimately reach a compromise, even if only a temporary one.

articles.title_orig: AI investors hedge against losses amid tech stock selloff
articles.title_zh: AI investors hedge against losses amid tech stock selloff
articles.content_orig:
Investor enthusiasm for artificial intelligence's potential to transform the global economy has fueled massive bets on the sector; however, growing concerns about a possible downturn are prompting investors to seek financial protection against losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday.
“We’re seeing really significant demand from folks looking to protect downside,” said Stephen Solaka, a senior vice president at Gateway Investment Advisers.
Investors and technology executives are increasingly turning to financial instruments such as put options and credit-default swaps to protect their investments.
Put options give investors the right to sell shares at a predetermined price before a specified date. For shareholders seeking protection, these contracts can limit potential losses if stock prices fall sharply, although investors must pay a premium for that protection.
A combination of rising borrowing costs for major data center projects and chip purchases, falling share prices among AI companies, and a broader stock market selloff has heightened concerns about the sector's financial outlook.
Friday's technology stock selloff wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value. The Nasdaq 100 index fell 3.4%, while the broader S&P 500 dropped 1.8%. The S&P 500's technology sector was hit particularly hard, declining more than 4.2%, NBC News reported Friday.
The growing demand for financial protection comes as AI companies continue seeking enormous amounts of capital to fund infrastructure development and expansion.
According to Solaka, some investors have accumulated such substantial gains from technology stocks that they now prioritize protecting their wealth over pursuing further returns.
“These people have made so much money, they’re quitting to hedge their stock,” Solaka said, adding that some companies restrict employees’ trades.
For example, trading in put options tied to AI cloud infrastructure company CoreWeave surged to record levels in October and remained elevated, according to data from Cboe Global Markets.
Investors are also turning to credit-default swaps, financial contracts that protect against a borrower failing to repay its debt.
According to the report, the cost of insuring against debt defaults by major technology companies, including Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle, rose over the past month to its highest level since 2021.
“There were no exceptions, suggesting broad market concern about the sector rather than idiosyncratic credit events at individual companies,” said Eugene Grinberg, a co-founder of bond data provider Solve.
As investment in AI infrastructure grows, trading firm Jump Trading has begun offering financial contracts that allow companies to protect themselves against a potential collapse in the price of computing power.
For example, companies renting out Nvidia chips could use these contracts to lock in a minimum rental price, protecting revenue if demand for AI computing power falls.
The growing demand for financial protection is reminiscent of the events depicted in The Big Short , when investors used credit-default swaps to bet against mortgage-backed securities before the 2008 financial crisis. Unlike those investors, however, many of today's technology shareholders are not necessarily betting on a market collapse, but seeking to protect gains accumulated during the AI boom.

articles.title_zh: Iran vows response beyond Mideast and target financial assets; oil markets fear generational damage
articles.content_orig:
The clock is ticking toward a new round of fighting in the U.S.-Iran war, but this time the damage could be much more widespread, stretching to new regions and different types of targets.
President Donald Trump has said he’s contemplating “another little Epic Fury” after the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.
The U.S. has already sent a third aircraft carrier and Marine expeditionary unit to the Middle East, and told allies in the region to prepare for a possible short but intense renewal of fighting, according to the Wall Street Journal .
The Iranian regime similarly stepped up its threats on how it would respond, seeking to deter an attack by threatening disproportionate and no-holds-barred retaliation.
On Saturday, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned Iran’s response would be “without any geographical limitations,” adding that the “data bank of targets should be updated so that the armed forces could hit all kinds of financial and non-financial assets.”
In recent weeks, Iran has warned undersea internet cables and data centers would be targets. The foiled attack on a British air base used by U.S. forces has also been attributed to Tehran.
And while North Koreans have been blamed for the $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance, it shows how vulnerable such assets are to Iran, which is also adept at cyberattacks. At the same time, the Pentagon is investigating whether hackers hit freezers on U.S. military bases .
The RAND think tank pointed out last week that hostile Iranian activity “spans the globe,” with proxy Hezbollah in Latin America and reported plots against civilians in Europe.
“Unbound and bent on revenge, Iran is unlikely to be contained to just one corner of the globe,” analysts wrote, arguing that the least bad option would be for the U.S. to continue its naval blockade and not launch new attacks.
Diplomacy is ongoing with the U.S. and Iran exchanging messages via intermediaries, but neither side has budged from their initial demands, dampening hopes for a breakthrough in the next few days.
Given the hardened rhetoric from the regime with threats of unrestricted retaliation, experts now detect a change in Iran’s tactics against the U.S. and see greater odds of the war returning.
For Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, the most important development was the message from Khamenei.
“This language suggests a further evolution in Iran’s military strategy,” he posted on X on Saturday. “Since the beginning of the war, Tehran has increasingly moved away from its traditional emphasis on proportionate response and retaliation toward a more offensive approach aimed at imposing costs on adversaries. The latest statements appear to take this logic a step further.”
Azizi also cited remarks from another top official who indicated Iran could stage a preemptive strike if preparations for hostile action were confirmed. In addition, Khamenei insisted Iran would determine when and how any renewed conflict ends.
Iran is also wary of further diplomatic efforts, especially since previous attacks came even in the middle of talks with the U.S. early this year and last summer.
“Iran appears increasingly determined to prevent a repetition of previous scenarios in which negotiations or temporary ceasefires were followed by renewed military conflict,” Azizi added. “From Tehran’s perspective, the objective is to make another attack so costly and unpredictable that Washington would have to reconsider the option altogether.”
Meanwhile, Iran still has thousands of missiles and drones in its arsenal that can inflict catastrophic damage to its neighbors in the Persian Gulf area.
That’s as stockpiles of U.S. interceptors have already been depleted to critically low levels, while newer Iranian missiles has demonstrated the ability to evade air-defense systems.
Considering how much damage the region’s energy infrastructure sustained earlier in the war, it can’t absorb another round of fighting, according to Amir Handjani is a board member at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Indeed, even U.S. military bases across the Middle East have been heavily damaged by Iranian drones and missiles.
“Gulf producers spent five decades persuading the world that their supply could withstand regional wars. Eight months of fighting on two fronts have badly weakened that case. A negotiated end to the war would give the region time to rebuild it,” Handjani wrote.
“Another round, on top of the Saudi-Houthi war, would leave damage to infrastructure and to importers’ confidence that markets are likely to carry for a generation.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Braces for Biggest Treasury Sales Overhaul in Years
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Braces for Biggest Treasury Sales Overhaul in Years
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Treasury Department will release its quarterly refunding statement on Wednesday, and markets are watching closely to see whether it adjusts its US Treasury issuance guidance. After Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unexpectedly signaled a willingness to intervene in the bond market to push down yields, dealers widely expect this could be the biggest adjustment to US Treasury issuance guidance since early 2024.
For more than two years, the Treasury has maintained in its quarterly statements that medium- and long-term Treasury issuance would remain stable. A change in this week's statement could pave the way for cutting 20-year and 30-year bond issuance in 2027 while expanding auctions of Treasury bills and shorter-dated notes. Citigroup predicts the Treasury will begin reducing 20-year and 30-year bond sales this month, which would effectively contravene the guidance given in the last quarterly refunding statement. Notably, about two weeks after that statement was released (Aug. 19), Bessent unexpectedly expanded long-bond buybacks, raising the per-operation cap from $2 billion to at least $4 billion — a move the market at the time saw as a response to surging yields.
April LaRusse, head of the investment specialists team at Insight Investment, said in an interview that the buyback sizes are too small to really change market direction. "If you're running the U.S. Treasury and your primary tool is issuance, then when you don't like where yields are, you adjust issuance," she said bluntly.
Any major adjustment would come as long-end yields have retreated from more than two-decade highs in early October. Still, the 30-year US Treasury bond yield remained above 5.30% on Friday, close to levels seen in mid-August when Bessent expanded the buyback program.
Relying further on Treasury bills maturing in one year or less to meet financing needs could ultimately test investors' capacity to absorb supply. Treasury bills mature quickly and must be constantly rolled over; the U.S. currently auctions more than $500 billion a week, leaving the Treasury highly vulnerable to sharp market swings. Last week, the Treasury's auction volume hit a record $839 billion.
Phoebe White, head of U.S. rates strategy at UBS Group, said adjusting the issuance strategy is "more likely to be a change in guidance than immediate action." But she also noted that the Treasury's recent "unconventional" behavior does "increase the likelihood that its actions will continue to deviate from historical precedent." UBS expects actual issuance sizes to remain unchanged until May next year.
The Treasury already opened the door to a guidance adjustment in August. At the time, officials made a subtle change to the guidance, saying they were assessing possible "changes" in future coupon-bearing and floating-rate note sales, where the previous language referred to potential "increases."
